newsitem.title: GERMANY: DASA teams up with Lagardere.
newsitem.headline: DASA teams up with Lagardere.

text.p: Germany's Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG (DASA) and France's Lagardere said on Wednesday they had signed a strategic cooperation agreement covering missiles, space and defence electronics.

In a joint statement issued by DASA's Munich headquarters, the companies said DASA would give its "total and unconditional support" for Lagardere's bid to buy Thomson-CSF, which is being offered for privatisation in France.
A DASA spokesman said, however, that did not mean that if Lagardere lost out in the two-horse race with Alcatel Altshom to buy Thomson that the deal would be scrapped.
"This agreement is stable," DASA spokesman Christian Breitsprecher told Reuters by telephone from Munich.

The statement said that the signing of a memorandum of understanding between DASA, a unit of auto giant Daimler-Benz, and defence-to-publishing group Lagardere was vital in the face of mounting North American competition.

"This Europe-wide consolidation is of critical necessity in order to be able to face increasing competition from the American industry, which has already been restructured into a few major groups," it said.
The pact also widens Lagardere's partnerships beyond its existing alliances with British Aerospace and GEC into a three-country grouping.
In the area of space cooperation, the activities of Matra Marconi Space (MMS) -- a venture owned 51 percent by Lagardere and 49 percent by GEC -- will be combined with DASA's.
The cooperation would cover satellites, launch vehicles and orbital infrastructure.
DASA and MMS will be equal partners in a business with worldwide sales of $3 billion, ranking it third in the world behind Lockheed Martin Corp and Boeing Corp.
"With that the German space industry is excellently positioned in the process of European restructuring," DASA chief executive Manfred Bischoff said in a separate statement.
In missiles, Matra BAe Dynamics -- a joint venture between Lagardere and British Aerospace -- will take a 30 percent stake in DASA unit LFK and become its strategic partner.

The deal should open DASA's business, hit by a tight German defence budget, to foreign markets and tie it in to Europe's leading missiles grouping. It would also leave room over for consolidation in the German missiles industry.
"Joining LFK to this strategically leading consortium will give new impulses to our traditional work with project partners in Europe and abroad," Bischoff commented.
In defence electronics, DASA and Lagardere intend to combine certain areas of their defence electronics businesses in several steps to create a company of equal partners.
Aerospace analysts welcomed the deal, saying it marked a long-overdue step towards defence consolidation in Europe.
"It is a small, but relatively encouraging step in terms of trying to create a large pan-European grouping," said Sash Tusa at UBS in London.

The deal may also be welcomed by Daimler-Benz shareholders since it will help DASA move out of non-core businesses and focus on its plane-making activities. DASA is a member of the Airbus passenger aircraft and Eurofighter combat jet projects.

Earlier, Lagardere and engineering group Alcatel said they had both submitted firm and final offers to buy the 58 percent state holding in Thomson-CSF. A decision is not expected until after Frances May 25 and June 1 general election.
British Aerospace said it had put 300 million pounds into the Lagardere offer, while GEC had signed memoranda of understanding with both bidders.
Breitsprecher declined to comment on any financial element of DASA's support for Lagardere's Thomson bid.
Asked on the prospects for winning the privatisation tender he said: "We see the chances as good, otherwise we would not have made this decision."
